title: The kill switch for harmful genes - Works in Progress Magazine
gist: siRNA gene-silencing has moved from concept to FDA-approved reality: after decades of chemistry work, temporarily switching off a precise gene in the liver is now a solved problem treatable with as few as four doses a year, and the field is racing to extend the same 'programmable medicine' platform to the kidneys, lungs, muscle, and brain.

insights.claim: The majority of human proteins are considered 'undruggable' because no synthesizable small molecule can effectively bind them, so conventional drug discovery is confined to the minority of druggable targets.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Platforms that bypass the small-molecule constraint expand the addressable disease universe far beyond legacy pharma pipelines, a structural tailwind for RNA and gene-editing companies.
insights.quote: The majority of human proteins are considered ‘undruggable’, meaning that none of the small molecules we can currently synthesize can effectively bind to them
insights.locator: It’s worse than this: medicinal chemists struggle

insights.claim: Poor prediction of small-molecule behavior in the body is a major reason most drugs fail in clinical trials, and even successful drugs may work for a different reason than originally hypothesized.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: High attrition is the core cost driver in pharma; technologies that tie mechanism directly to biology could compress trial-failure risk and R&D spend.
insights.locator: Even for those targets, success is far from guaranteed

insights.claim: siRNA is a short RNA strand that binds a matching mRNA sequence like a barcode and targets it for destruction by the cell's gene-silencing machinery, so if the mRNA is destroyed the disease-causing protein is never built.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: The mechanism lets a single chemistry platform target any protein whose sequence is known, decoupling treatment discovery from per-target chemistry.
insights.locator: That’s exactly what siRNA, or ‘small interfering RNA’, does

insights.claim: The 1990 discovery of gene silencing came by accident when scientists at DNA Plant Technology Corporation added a pigment gene to petunias to darken them but the extra copy turned the flowers white, an effect they named 'cosuppression'.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: The Nobel-winning origin story underscores how foundational the mechanism is; the biology is decades-mature even though delivery only recently became viable.
insights.locator: The story of siRNA begins in 1990

themes.theme: The delivery problem and lipid nanoparticles

insights.claim: Naked siRNA injected into veins fails on three counts: enzymes destroy unprotected RNA, it cannot reach target mRNA without entering a cell, and cell entry via an endosome exposes it to digestive enzymes.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Delivery, not biology, was the decades-long gating problem; whoever solves delivery for a new organ unlocks that organ's entire disease market.
insights.locator: The delivery problem

insights.claim: Ionizable lipids solved endosomal escape by staying neutral in the bloodstream to minimize damage and turning positive inside acidic endosomes to rupture the membrane and release the siRNA.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: This chemistry underpins both siRNA and mRNA-vaccine delivery, making ionizable-lipid IP a durable moat across the RNA-medicine sector.
insights.locator: The next breakthrough was more subtle

insights.claim: It took more than a decade of tinkering with ionizable lipid chemistry, yielding a thousand-fold improvement in potency, to make lipid nanoparticles that were stable, taken up by cells, and could escape endosomes safely.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: The thousand-fold optimization curve shows how much accumulated process knowledge sits behind approved products, a barrier to fast-follower competitors.
insights.locator: Even after coming up with that basic idea

themes.theme: Approved drugs and Alnylam's naked siRNA

insights.claim: The FDA approved the first RNA interference drug, patisiran, in 2018 to treat nerve damage from hereditary transthyretin amyloidosis, delivering siRNA in lipid nanoparticles to silence the mutated gene in liver cells.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: First-approval milestone validated the class commercially; investors can date the platform's clinical proof to 2018.
insights.locator: In 2018, the FDA approved

insights.claim: Alnylam Pharmaceuticals made siRNA sturdy enough to survive naked in the body by chemically modifying RNA's reactive oxygen atom, swapping it for fluorine or hydrogen or adding a methyl group for almost indefinite protection against degradation.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Chemical stabilization eliminated the need for lipid carriers, a step-change in dosing convenience that reshaped the competitive frontier.
insights.locator: Naked siRNA

insights.claim: Naked siRNA is guided to the liver by attaching three copies of a GalNAc sugar, which liver-cell surface receptors recognize and bring inside, replacing the passive liver accumulation that lipid nanoparticles achieved by mimicking cholesterol.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Targeting via molecular 'address labels' is the generalizable template for extending siRNA beyond the liver, the key value-creation lever ahead.
insights.locator: With stability solved, the next challenge

insights.claim: Endosomal escape for naked siRNA turned out to require no engineering: under one percent of the molecule fluke-leaks from the endosome over time, but siRNA is so potent that very little is needed for a gene-silencing effect.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Extreme potency is why sub-1% delivery efficiency still yields durable drugs, explaining the class's remarkable dosing intervals.
insights.quote: The proportion of siRNA leaking out of endosomes can be well under one percent, but often that is enough because siRNA is so potent
insights.locator: That left the final hurdle of escaping the endosome

insights.claim: Patisiran, carried by a lipid nanoparticle, must be dosed every three weeks, while Alnylam's naked GalNAc siRNA drug vutrisiran treats the same condition but is dosed only once every three months, with other GalNAc siRNA drugs needing only twice-yearly dosing.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Radically longer dosing intervals drive adherence and pricing power, and made the lipid-nanoparticle approach commercially obsolete for the same indication.
insights.locator: The result is a massive difference in how long the drug lasts

insights.claim: GalNAc siRNA drugs avoid the immune-reaction risk of lipid nanoparticles, so patients no longer need immunosuppressants that patisiran required alongside treatment.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: A cleaner safety profile widens eligible patient populations and reduces treatment complexity, reinforcing the naked-siRNA advantage.
insights.locator: GalNAc siRNA drugs also have another advantage

insights.claim: Multiple siRNA drugs are already approved for liver diseases including amyloidosis, hemophilia, high cholesterol, and acute hepatic porphyria, with late-stage trials underway for high blood pressure, diabetes, and fatty liver disease.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: The pipeline is expanding from rare into large chronic-disease markets, materially enlarging the commercial opportunity for the class.
insights.locator: Multiple siRNA drugs have been approved

themes.theme: Beyond the liver: the brain race

insights.claim: Swapping the GalNAc liver-targeting sugar for other molecules is how the field aims to direct siRNA to the kidneys, lungs, fat tissue, muscle, and brain, with startups like Manifold Bio and Soufflé Therapeutics competing.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Organ-targeting IP is the next competitive battleground; each solved organ is effectively a new market, drawing well-funded startup entrants.
insights.locator: That’s exactly what the field is now trying to do

insights.claim: Alnylam's Alzheimer's program targets the amyloid precursor protein while Arrowhead's targets tau, reflecting the two intervention points implied by the amyloid hypothesis.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Two named competitors are pursuing distinct mechanistic bets on the largest CNS market, a binary catalyst set for both companies.
insights.locator: Alnylam’s program targets the amyloid precursor, while Arrowhead’s targets tau

insights.claim: The two brain programs diverge on delivery: Alnylam bypasses the blood-brain barrier with intrathecal spinal injection of fatty-acid-attached siRNA, while Arrowhead attempts a subcutaneous injection of a proprietary molecule meant to cross the barrier itself.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Arrowhead's less invasive route, if it works, would be far more patient-friendly for chronic dosing; delivery route is a key differentiator to track.
insights.locator: The most immediate is accessing the brain

insights.claim: By the time Alzheimer's is diagnosed the brain damage is often extensive enough that clearing amyloid plaques has little effect, so even successful siRNA delivery and a correct amyloid hypothesis may not translate into meaningful slowing of the disease.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Biology, not delivery, may cap Alzheimer's efficacy; a sober flag against over-pricing CNS siRNA trial optimism.
insights.quote: by the time Alzheimer’s disease is diagnosed, the damage to the brain is often extensive enough that clearing amyloid plaques has little effect on slowing its progress
insights.locator: Even if the amyloid hypothesis is correct

insights.claim: Once chemists solve delivery to an organ, treating a new disease of that organ requires only specifying a new RNA or DNA sequence while holding the chemistry constant, so vutrisiran and the cholesterol drug inclisiran (which targets PCSK9) work by identical principles.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Platform economics mean marginal cost of a new indication is low once delivery is solved, implying rapid pipeline expansion per solved organ.
insights.quote: all that’s required to treat a new disease of that organ is to specify a new RNA or DNA sequence while holding the chemistry constant
insights.locator: The future of programmable medicines

insights.claim: siRNA is one of several programmable-medicine platforms alongside antisense oligonucleotides, mRNA vaccines, and CRISPR gene editing, each already with FDA-approved treatments and each linking biological understanding directly to medicine.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: The programmable-medicine category is broader than siRNA; investors should view these platforms as a connected wave rather than isolated bets.
insights.locator: The future of programmable medicines

insights.claim: An antisense oligonucleotide targeting the tau protein in Alzheimer's has shown promising results in a phase two clinical trial, offering a competing modality to siRNA for the same target.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: ASOs compete directly with siRNA on tau, so a CNS bet on one modality carries cross-modality risk.
insights.locator: antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) are short strands
